extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the Step 2B (inventive-concept / 'significantly more') analysis under the Alice/Mayo §101 framework, including how to identify and evaluate additional claim elements and what counts (or does not count) as an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that are not 'significantly more' — mere instructions to implement on a computer
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) with the judicial exception, or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer is not enough to qualify as 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a limitation indicating that a particular function such as creating and maintaining electronic records is performed by a computer. (Cited: Alice Corp.) See also MPEP § 2106.05(f). Mere recitation that a computer performs routine functions does not add an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that are not 'significantly more' — appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry, specified at a high level of generality, does not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim to an abstract idea requiring no more than a generic computer to perform generic functions; courts describe such computer functions as 'well-understood, routine, conventional activit[ies]'. (Alice Corp.; see MPEP § 2106.05(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that are not 'significantly more' — insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity (activity that does not meaningfully contribute an inventive concept) does not make a claim significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: mere data gathering in conjunction with a law of nature or abstract idea (e.g., obtaining information about credit card transactions solely so an abstract mental process can analyze it). (CyberSource v. Retail Decisions; MPEP § 2106.05(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that are not 'significantly more' — mere field-of-use or technological-environment linking
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use does not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: limiting abstract idea of hedging to commodities markets or limiting a mathematical formula to petrochemical fields. (Bilski; Parker v. Flook; see MPEP § 2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangibility/physicality is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element(s) is not a relevant consideration in Step 2B and does not automatically provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts: a computer is a tangible machine, but mere recitation of physical components (e.g., computer hardware) does not guarantee eligibility; physical steps (e.g., DNA amplification) do not necessarily provide sufficient inventive concept. Conversely, lack of physicality does not doom claims if there is a genuine improvement to technology (see Enfish, McRO, Genetic Technologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B evaluation method — identify and evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner should identify additional claim elements beyond the judicial exception(s), then evaluate those additional elements individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should reference Supreme Court considerations and MPEP §2106.05(a)-(h). The inquiry is not a weighing test — it's whether the additional elements, considered individually and in combination, contribute an inventive concept. See Alice and Mayo analyses and examples (Alice, BASCOM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Supreme Court / MPEP considerations as the basis for the analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Step 2B evaluation is made with respect to considerations the Supreme Court has identified as relevant to eligibility; examiners should consult the detailed considerations in MPEP §2106.05(a)-(h).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many considerations overlap; more than one may be relevant. Not all will apply to every element. Focus on whether the additional elements, relative to the applicant's invention, encompass an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims evaluated on a claim-by-claim basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately; similar claims should not be assumed to stand or fall together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dependent claim may be eligible if it recites additional elements that amount to significantly more even if the independent claim is ineligible. Consider each claim's particular elements and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiple judicial exceptions in a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless it is clear that the claim recites discrete exceptions, examiners should avoid parsing a claim into multiple exceptions; if multiple discrete exceptions are present, examiners may select one exception and conduct the analysis for efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If analysis for the selected exception finds an additional element or combination that amounts to significantly more, the claim should be considered patent eligible. If not, consider rejection. (Cited: University of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome rule for Step 2B (Pathway C vs ineligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception, the claim is eligible (Pathway C) and eligibility analysis ends; if not, the claim is not patent-eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPEP §2106.07 for formulating an ineligibility rejection. 'Significantly more' is judged with respect to the claim as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement-to-technology consideration (improvement to computer/functioning or other technical field)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should consider whether the claim purports to improve the functioning of the computer itself or any other technology or technical field — i.e., whether it presents a technological solution to a technological problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration can be evaluated at Step 2A or Step 2B and supports streamlined analyses when self-evident. Key cases: DDR Holdings, Enfish, Amdocs, McRO, Visual Memory. See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification support requirement for asserted technological improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention is asserted to improve conventional computer functioning or technology, the specification must provide a technical explanation (sufficient detail) showing how to implement the improvement such that one of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: discussion of a technical problem and an unconventional technical solution, or identification of technical improvements over prior art. Lack of such details (e.g., Affinity Labs) weighs against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must reflect the disclosed improvement and be evaluated under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the specification discloses an improvement, the claim itself must reflect that improvement when considered under BRI; examiners must consider the claim as a whole (ordered combination) and avoid oversimplification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim's full scope does not capture the improvement described in the specification, eligibility may not be shown (e.g., Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec). Evaluate specific claim requirements, not just general statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement must be to a particular solution/way of achieving an outcome rather than merely claiming an idea/outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that covers a particular solution or particular way to achieve a desired outcome is more likely to show an improvement to technology than one that merely claims the idea of a solution or an outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have relied on specificity of claimed solution (e.g., McRO: particular rules for animation) to find claims directed to technological improvements rather than abstract ideas. Overlap exists with particular_machine and mere_instructions considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators that a claim improves computer functionality (positive examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain specific kinds of changes indicate an improvement to computer functionality (not exhaustive): modifications to protocols, inventive distribution of functionality, methods of rendering images, unconventional distributed architectures to reduce congestion, configurable memory systems, technical details for image transmission, particular server structures, specific programming/design methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court-cited examples: (i) DDR Holdings: modified hyperlink protocol; (ii) BASCOM: inventive distribution for filtering; (iii) Research Corp.: halftone rendering; (iv) Amdocs/Openet: unconventional distributed network architecture; (v) Visual Memory: configurable memory system; (vi) TLI Communications: technical transmission/classification details (lack of details can make claims ineligible); (vii) TLI Communications: particular server structure; (viii) Apple v. Ameranth: particular way of programming menus. Use these as guidance but assess each claim's specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that computer-implemented method claims must be limited to computer implementation to show computer-functionality improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: For a method claim to be considered an improvement to computer functionality, its BRI must limit the claim to computer implementation; if the claim's entire scope can be performed mentally or verbally, it cannot be said to improve computer technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Synopsys (method could be performed without a computer), RecogniCorp (encoding/decoding process did not require a computer). If embodiments exist that can be practiced without a computer, the improvement consideration may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples that may not be sufficient to show improvement (negative examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain claimed benefits or uses are unlikely to show an improvement to computer functionality if they rely only on general-purpose computer capabilities or automation of manual processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court-cited non-sufficient examples: (i) generating restaurant menus with functionally claimed features (Ameranth); (ii) speeding data analysis solely from general-purpose computer capabilities (FairWarning); (iii) merely using a computer to perform an abstract idea (Return Mail); (iv) mere automation of manual processes like generic loan-application processing (Credit Acceptance, LendingTree); (v) recording/transmitting/archiving images using conventional/generic tech without showing inventive solution (TLI Communications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to other technology/technical fields can show eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements outside of computer functionality — i.e., to other technologies or technical fields — can also demonstrate patent eligibility when the claim recites a particular technical advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples include: (i) computerized method operating a rubber molding press with thermocouple monitoring (Diehr); (ii) new telephone/server combinations (TLI Communications); (iii) advances in downloading for streaming (Affinity Labs); (iv) specific digital data compression methods (DDR Holdings, Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec); (v) integrating virus screening into the Internet (Symantec); (vi) components/methods that generate new data (Electric Power Group v. Alstom); (vii) particular configuration and methods for inertial sensors (Thales Visionix). Use these examples to recognize technological improvements beyond general computing.
